title: NLP Tasks and Evaluation
description: Measure language systems and understand translation, retrieval, and dialogue tasks.

questions.prompt: What does BLEU primarily compare in machine translation evaluation?
questions.explanation: BLEU uses modified n-gram precision and a brevity penalty; it does not fully capture meaning or fluency.

questions.prompt: A high BLEU score guarantees that a translation preserves the intended meaning.
questions.explanation: Overlap metrics can miss semantic errors and may penalize valid paraphrases.

questions.prompt: ROUGE is commonly used to compare generated summaries with references using what?
questions.explanation: ROUGE variants measure overlap such as n-grams or longest common subsequences, but have known limitations.

questions.prompt: What does exact match measure in a question-answering evaluation?
options: Whether the normalized prediction matches a reference exactly
questions.explanation: Exact match is strict and easy to interpret but can score valid paraphrases as incorrect.

questions.prompt: Which are useful ways to analyze an NLP model’s errors?
questions.explanation: Slice-based and qualitative review reveals failure patterns hidden by a single aggregate score.

questions.prompt: Why split NLP data by document or source when leakage is possible?
options: Near-duplicate text can otherwise appear in both train and test
questions.explanation: Grouping related or duplicated documents prevents overly optimistic evaluation from shared content.

questions.prompt: What is word alignment in machine translation?
options: Associate source-language units with corresponding target-language units
questions.explanation: Alignment identifies approximate correspondences between words or phrases across parallel text.

questions.prompt: A parallel corpus contains texts that are translations of one another.
questions.explanation: Parallel corpora pair source text with target-language translations and support translation learning or evaluation.

questions.prompt: In information retrieval, what is a ranking function used for?
options: Order candidate documents by estimated relevance to a query
questions.explanation: Ranking functions score candidates so likely relevant documents appear earlier in results.

questions.prompt: What does normalized discounted cumulative gain account for?
options: Graded relevance and the position of results in a ranking
Only whether the first result is exactly correct
The training loss of a classifier
questions.explanation: NDCG gives more credit to relevant results near the top and can handle graded relevance.

questions.prompt: Which metrics can evaluate ranked retrieval results?
options: BLEU score as a default ranking metric
questions.explanation: Precision@k, MRR, and NDCG evaluate ranked results in different ways; BLEU is for text generation comparison.

questions.prompt: What does dialogue-state tracking estimate?
options: The current relevant entities, intents, or slot values in a conversation
questions.explanation: Dialogue state summarizes task-relevant information accumulated from prior turns.

questions.prompt: In a task-oriented assistant, intent classification predicts what?
options: The user’s goal, such as booking or checking status
The number of words in a response
questions.explanation: Intent labels capture the action or purpose expressed by a user utterance.

questions.prompt: Slot filling extracts structured values such as a date or destination from an utterance.
questions.explanation: A dialogue system can populate slots from recognized entities and attributes in user text.

questions.prompt: What is abstractive summarization?
options: Generate a concise summary that may use wording absent from the source
Classify each source token by part of speech
Translate a summary into the same language
questions.explanation: Abstractive systems compose new text, unlike extractive methods that select source spans.

questions.prompt: What makes automatic summary evaluation challenging?
options: Multiple valid summaries can express the same content
Lexical overlap can miss factual errors
A reference set may cover only some valid wording
Summary length is the only quality dimension
questions.explanation: Meaning, factuality, and valid paraphrase are not captured by a single overlap score or length.

questions.prompt: Which task is usually part of spoken-language processing rather than text-only NLP?
questions.explanation: Speech recognition converts an audio signal into text; downstream NLP may then analyze the transcript.

questions.prompt: When is human evaluation especially useful for language generation?
options: When qualities such as helpfulness or factual support are hard to capture automatically
Only when there is no reference text
questions.explanation: Human judgments can assess nuanced qualities, though protocols need clear rubrics and reliability checks.

questions.prompt: Inter-annotator agreement can help reveal ambiguity or inconsistency in labeling guidelines.
questions.explanation: Agreement statistics and disagreement review help assess how consistently annotators apply a scheme.

questions.prompt: Why evaluate NLP systems separately across languages?
options: Data, scripts, morphology, and performance can vary by language
All languages use the same token distribution
One language’s score proves all others
questions.explanation: Language-specific resources and properties can produce uneven quality, requiring appropriate per-language evaluation.
